From Left and Right, American Populism Is Coming for Corporate America
 
Plus, why the GOP pins its Senate hopes on New Hampshire, and threat of Iranian drone attack prompts U.S. to fly its B-1 bombers out of U.K.
 
 
CARLOS BARRIA/REUTERS
 

Good morning. There’s a political horseshoe forming.

 

Voters from the left and the right are finding a common, populist ground targeting American corporations. And this anger is going beyond just Big Tech. 

 

There is a growing embrace of a bigger government role that could crack down on credit-card companies, healthcare companies, housing and child care.

 

Some Republicans have suggested certain CEOs are paid too much. And some Democrats see it as a badge of honor to attempt to evict companies from the political process. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, has made removing corporate influence from politics a primary goal of his campaign.

 

Fairly or unfairly, there is a broad frustration from voters in both parties that government policies have pushed prices higher.

 

This has been building for a while. Both the Biden and Trump administrations have gone after beef and energy companies, for example, places where rising prices have drawn loud complaints.

 

There are now unusual alliances that backed many Democrats and Republicans into a corner on things like artificial intelligence. But American businesses could see this energy only escalate in 2027 and 2028, when both political parties host open primaries and loud, populist voices will be calling for big changes. 

 

Things like tariffs and even corporate tax increases, which used to be politically tough, might be back on the table.

 

American businesses have a long legacy of supporting lawmakers from both parties to help shape Washington’s agenda. But it’s possible that the political center of the country has moved outside of Washington now, to places where this influence isn’t as salient.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

J. Dennis Hastert: The former Republican House speaker, who went from being one of the nation’s most powerful politicians to serving a federal prison sentence, has died.

 

President Trump’s Tuesday: Trump is expected to hold policy meetings at 11 a.m. ET and 12:30 p.m. Next, he will participate in a Gold Star Families reception at 1 p.m., and then depart for Maryland, where he is set to deliver remarks at a shipyard at 4 p.m.

What I’m Following

 
 
EMILIO MUSTO FOR WSJ
 

Republicans pin their hope for the Senate on another New Hampshire Sununu. John Sununu’s bid for a political comeback could act as a lifeline in the GOP’s quest to cling to its teetering Senate majority. He will need to navigate a narrow political tightrope, creating enough distance from Trump in a difficult political environment while still attracting MAGA supporters.

 

A threat of an Iranian drone attack prompted the U.S. to pull bombers from a U.K. base. The U.S. military moved a dozen B-1 bomber aircraft from a U.K. military base on Sunday because of concerns about a possible drone attack ordered by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, according to American and European officials briefed on the incident.

 

The Treasury Department has transformed children’s Trump Accounts. The Treasury recently enabled auto-enrollment and stock donations for the program, turning it into a universal child-investment vehicle. The catch? Kids and their parents can’t pick the stocks or reject donated shares, and they can’t sell for five years.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Trump will pay for controversial pro-Trump television ads using funds from his MAGA Inc. super PAC rather than the federal government.

 

• The Supreme Court has questions about oil companies’ efforts to shut down climate lawsuits.

 

• Oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz once more—but it isn’t the kind the world needs.
